h1:
Songkhla Local Breakfast
Dim Sum, Rice Stew & Old-School Coffee
intro: If you want to understand Songkhla and Hat Yai on a deeper level, set your alarm early — breakfast is the meal locals take most seriously here. Freshly steamed dim sum baskets, rich dark rice stew with a massive steamed bao, and drip-bag coffee in a century-old shophouse on Songkhla's heritage streets. This is what people here have been eating since before dawn.

blocks.html: Hat Yai and Songkhla's breakfast culture carries a strong Hokkien-Chinese imprint — the legacy of Chinese settlers who arrived by boat and put down roots here centuries ago. Dim sum is no novelty; it's a normal family breakfast where everyone pulls up a chair, pours hot tea, and works through bamboo baskets together. Over in Songkhla's old town, you'll find century-old rice stew recipes and kopitiam coffee passed down through multiple generations. We've split this into three categories — dim sum, rice stew, and old-school coffee — with spots that are genuinely open right now.

blocks.title: Read Before You Go
blocks.html: Breakfast here starts early and wraps up fast. Several of Hat Yai's best-known dim sum shops open at 5:30 AM and sell out before noon. If you have a specific place in mind, aim to arrive before 8 AM to avoid disappointment. Many shops are cash only — bring small bills.

blocks.text: Dim Sum — Breakfast That Hat Yai Takes Seriously

blocks.html: Hat Yai is the real dim sum capital of southern Thailand. Small bamboo baskets stacked high on steaming carts hold everything from siu mai and har gow to steamed bao, braised pork trotters, and a pot of bak kut teh simmered with Chinese herbal spices. Per-basket prices are still very easy on the wallet — starting around THB 17–25 — and three or four people can walk away full for well under a few hundred baht. These are the spots locals actually go to, with queues forming before the sun is fully up.

items.name: Dimsum Nak Wing
items.blurb: The dim sum spot many locals call their default Hat Yai breakfast. Baskets come out freshly steamed and hot, with a balanced savoury-sweet flavour. They also do bak kut teh and roti with curry — a red shophouse in a modern-Chinese style with decent street parking. Opens at 5:30 AM for serious early risers.
items.meta: Niphat Songkhro 1 Rd, Soi 2 (behind Hat Yai City Municipality) · Opens approx. 05.30–11.30

items.name: Kuk Chai Dim Sum
items.blurb: A legendary Hat Yai institution — tables fill up fast from the morning rush, and you may need to share one. Every basket is steamed fresh. Beyond the classics, their bak kut teh, steamed sea bass with sauce, and pan-fried bao stand out. Weekends can mean a short wait, but it moves quickly.
items.meta: Thung Sao 1 Soi, Hat Yai · Open 06.00–13.00 daily

items.name: Marita Dim Sum Halal
items.blurb: Halal dim sum for Muslim visitors and anyone avoiding pork. Full menu including chicken siu mai, steamed bao, and hot tea. An option you won't easily find in most other Thai cities.
items.meta: Hat Yai city area · Opens in the morning

items.name: Nad Kafae Dim Sum
items.blurb: A breakfast spot known for its fragrant bak kut teh brewed with Chinese herbal spices — best eaten alongside a few baskets of dim sum and a cup of coffee. Relaxed atmosphere; good for a long, easy morning conversation.
items.meta: Hat Yai city area · Opens approx. 06.00–11.30 daily

items.name: Chok Dee Tae Tiam
items.blurb: A veteran Hokkien-style tae tiam (Chinese tea restaurant) that has been in Hat Yai's city centre for decades. Good if you want a traditional Chinese breakfast experience beyond just bamboo baskets.
items.meta: Hat Yai city centre · Opens in the morning

blocks.title: Eat Dim Sum Like a Local
blocks.html: Order a pot of hot Chinese tea the moment you sit down, then pick baskets from the cart as it comes round. Hat Yai regulars usually order one shared pot of bak kut teh, eaten with fried garlic and chilli soy sauce on the side. Don't overeat at the first stop — rice stew and coffee are still waiting.

blocks.text: Rice Stew — A True Songkhla Old Town Dish

blocks.html: Cross from Hat Yai to Songkhla old town — about 30 km — and you'll find a dish most visitors haven't heard of: khao satu (rice stew). It's rice topped with slow-braised beef or pork in a deep brown broth, rich with a sweet-savoury balance that shows both Western and Chinese influence — a flavour you can only really find here. Eat it with an oversized steamed bao for one of the most filling breakfasts the south has to offer.

items.name: Khao Satu Kiad Fang — Nang Ngam Road
items.blurb: The first rice stew shop in Songkhla, open since 1937, sitting on Nang Ngam Road in the old town. The broth is thick and concentrated; you can add crispy pork and Chinese sausage. The giant steamed bao is the thing not to miss — a signature that's kept people coming back for generations.
items.meta: Nang Ngam Rd, Songkhla Old Town · Rice stew 07.00–13.00 / Steamed bao 10.30–17.00 · Closed on Buddhist holy days and Thursdays
items.price: Rice stew with extras ~THB 140 · Steamed bao from ~THB 25 each

items.name: Khao Satu Na Suan
items.blurb: A rice stew shop next to Hat Yai's municipal park — a decent option if you're based on the Hat Yai side and don't want to drive all the way to Songkhla old town. Approachable flavour, easy to get to, opens in the morning.
items.meta: Near Hat Yai Municipality Park · Opens in the morning

items.name: Khao Satu Ad — Chiranakhon Branch
items.blurb: An early-opening rice stew shop in the Chiranakhon neighbourhood of Hat Yai. Straightforward and budget-friendly — fine for anyone wanting a taste of the dish without the drive into Songkhla old town.
items.meta: Chiranakhon area, Hat Yai · Opens very early

blocks.html: Honestly, Kiad Fang should be your first stop if you're heading into Songkhla old town — you get the original recipe and the atmosphere of a historic shophouse all at once. The one thing to watch out for: they close on Buddhist holy days and Thursdays, so check the calendar before you go. If you're short on time and staying in Hat Yai, Na Suan or Ad will give you a reasonable taste of the dish without the detour.

blocks.text: Old-School Coffee — Slow Sips in a Heritage Shophouse

blocks.html: Round off your morning with old-school coffee — the quiet charm that makes Songkhla old town worth a full morning on its own. Nang Ngam Road, Nakhon Nok Road, and Nakhon Nai Road are lined with Sino-Portuguese and Chinese shophouses that are close to a century old, and several have opened as coffee shops. Some are traditional kopitiam brewing through a cloth sock; others are newer cafés that happen to occupy spectacular old buildings. Either way, it's a spot to sit with an iced coffee or hot brew and not rush anywhere.

items.name: Ong Hiab Huat
items.blurb: A coffee shop inside a heritage shophouse in Songkhla old town. Classic atmosphere — come for the bitter coffee and the antiques, stay to soak up the sense of a city that hasn't moved on too fast. Open approx. 10.00–18.00.

items.name: Nang Ngam Road Cafés
items.blurb: The whole street is lined with cafés occupying old shophouses. Wander and try one at a time — you'll find specialty coffee alongside street-art murals on the walls between buildings.

items.name: Kopitiam at the Morning Market
items.blurb: For a truly traditional coffee experience, look for kopitiam stalls inside Hat Yai and Songkhla morning markets. Brewed through a cloth bag, served as iced coffee (oliang) or hot — best with a side of pa thong ko (Chinese doughnuts).

blocks.title: A Straight-Up Heads-Up
blocks.html: Many old-town cafés open late — around 10 AM — so they won't work as a proper breakfast stop. If you want coffee early, find a kopitiam stall at the morning market or a dim sum shop that serves coffee on the side. Save the shophouse cafés for a mid-morning break after dim sum or rice stew; the timing works out better that way.
If you have a few days, try to work through all three categories — moving from the Hat Yai side out to Songkhla old town. This is a plan you can actually follow without renting a helicopter.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Full Hat Yai Dim Sum Morning

items.activity: Start at Dimsum Nak Wing or Kuk Chai Dim Sum
items.note: Arrive before 8 AM to skip the queue. Order hot Chinese tea and one shared pot of bak kut teh.

items.activity: Walk off breakfast at Hat Yai morning market
items.note: Find a kopitiam stall for old-school coffee with pa thong ko to wrap up the meal.

items.activity: Rest up — tomorrow heads to Songkhla old town
items.note: The drive from Hat Yai to Songkhla takes about 30–40 min.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Rice Stew & Old Town Coffee in Songkhla

items.activity: Khao Satu Kiad Fang, Nang Ngam Road
items.note: Confirm it's not a Buddhist holy day or Thursday first. Order with crispy pork extras and the oversized steamed bao.

items.activity: Stroll Nang Ngam – Nakhon Nok – Nakhon Nai roads
items.note: Take in the old shophouse architecture and street-art murals along the way.

items.activity: Coffee at Ong Hiab Huat or another heritage-shophouse café
items.note: No need to rush — this is a relaxed mid-morning break to close out the morning.

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Easy Day Close to Your Hotel

items.activity: Khao Satu Ad or Khao Satu Na Suan, in Hat Yai
items.note: Good for a later start or when you'd rather not travel far.

items.activity: Halal dim sum at Marita for pork-free option
items.note: Or try Chok Dee Tae Tiam for a more traditional Chinese-style breakfast experience.

items.activity: Find your favourite coffee shop to end the trip
items.note: Pick up some old-school ground coffee or local snacks to bring home.

faq.q: What does a typical Songkhla local breakfast look like?
faq.a: Three things define it: freshly steamed dim sum baskets in the Hat Yai style, thick dark-broth rice stew served with a giant steamed bao from Songkhla old town, and traditional kopitiam coffee brewed through a cloth bag at morning markets and heritage shophouse cafés.

faq.q: Where's the best dim sum in Hat Yai?
faq.a: The spots locals actually go to are Dimsum Nak Wing (opens at 5:30 AM) and Kuk Chai Dim Sum on Thung Sao 1 Soi — both get long queues in the morning, so aim to arrive before 8 AM. Muslim visitors have Marita Dim Sum Halal as a dedicated pork-free option.

faq.q: When does Khao Satu Kiad Fang open, and where exactly is it?
faq.a: It's on Nang Ngam Road in Songkhla old town. Rice stew is served from about 07.00–13.00; steamed bao from 10.30–17.00. The shop closes on Buddhist holy days and Thursdays, so check before you go. A plate with extras costs around THB 140; steamed bao start at THB 25 each.

faq.q: Where can I find old-school coffee in Songkhla?
faq.a: The Nang Ngam, Nakhon Nok, and Nakhon Nai road area of Songkhla old town has several cafés inside heritage shophouses — Ong Hiab Huat is a good first stop. Most open around 10 AM though, so for early-morning coffee, look for a kopitiam stall inside the morning market instead.

faq.q: What time should I show up for breakfast?
faq.a: The earlier the better. Popular dim sum shops open from 5:30–6:00 AM and often sell out before noon. We'd suggest starting your morning meal before 8 AM. Old-town shophouse cafés are a mid-morning affair — they open around 10 AM, which is perfect timing after dim sum or rice stew.
